raw: CHAPTER VIII. A Hand at Cards
en: [Chapter 8] A Hand at Cards

raw: Happily unconscious of the new calamity at home, Miss Pross threaded her way along the narrow streets and crossed the river by the bridge of the Pont-Neuf, reckoning in her mind the number of indispensable purchases she had to make.
en: Happily unaware of the new disaster at home, Miss Pross made her way through the narrow streets and crossed the river by the Pont-Neuf bridge, counting in her head the essential things she had to buy.

raw: Mr.
en: Jerry Cruncher walked at her side carrying the basket.

raw: Cruncher, with the basket, walked at her side.
en: They both looked left and right into the shops they passed, kept a careful eye out for any crowds, and took side paths to avoid excited groups of talkers.

raw: They both looked to the right and to the left into most of the shops they passed, had a wary eye for all gregarious assemblages of people, and turned out of their road to avoid any very excited group of talkers.
en: They both looked carefully into most of the shops they passed, keeping a watchful eye out for any large crowds, and even changed their route to avoid any loud or excited groups of people talking.

raw: It was a raw evening, and the misty river, blurred to the eye with blazing lights and to the ear with harsh noises, showed where the barges were stationed in which the smiths worked, making guns for the Army of the Republic.
en: The misty river was lit up with bright lights and filled with the harsh noise of metalworking barges, where blacksmiths were making guns for the Republic's army.

raw: Woe to the man who played tricks with _that_ Army, or got undeserved promotion in it!
en: Woe to anyone who crossed _that_ army or got a promotion they didn't deserve!

raw: Better for him that his beard had never grown, for the National Razor shaved him close.
en: It would have been better for him if his beard had never grown, for the Guillotine would cut his head off.

raw: Having purchased a few small articles of grocery, and a measure of oil for the lamp, Miss Pross bethought herself of the wine they wanted.
en: After buying a few groceries and some lamp oil, Miss Pross remembered they needed wine.

raw: After peeping into several wine-shops, she stopped at the sign of the Good Republican Brutus of Antiquity, not far from the National Palace, once (and twice) the Tuileries, where the aspect of things rather took her fancy.
en: After looking into several wine shops, she stopped at one called "The Good Republican Brutus of Antiquity" near the National Palace, which used to be the Tuileries Palace.

raw: It had a quieter look than any other place of the same description they had passed, and, though red with patriotic caps, was not so red as the rest.
en: It looked quieter than any of the similar shops they had walked by. Even though it was still full of red patriotic caps, it wasn't quite as red as the rest of the places.

raw: Sounding Mr.
en: Although it had some people in red caps inside, it didn't look as wild as the others.

raw: Cruncher, and finding him of her opinion, Miss Pross resorted to the Good Republican Brutus of Antiquity, attended by her cavalier.
en: Asking Jerry, and finding that he agreed, Miss Pross went inside, accompanied by her guard.

raw: Slightly observant of the smoky lights; of the people, pipe in mouth, playing with limp cards and yellow dominoes; of the one bare-breasted, bare-armed, soot-begrimed workman reading a journal aloud, and of the others listening to him; of the weapons worn, or laid aside to be resumed; of the two or three customers fallen forward asleep, who in the popular high-shouldered shaggy black spencer looked, in that attitude, like slumbering bears or dogs; the two outlandish customers approached the counter, and showed what they wanted.
en: The room was thick with smoky lamplight. Customers sat smoking pipes and fiddling with worn cards and yellow dominoes. A shirtless, soot-covered worker read a newspaper aloud to a small crowd. Weapons lay scattered around the tables. Two or three customers were slumped asleep, looking like sleeping bears in their heavy black coats. Taking all of this in, the two English customers walked up to the counter and showed what they wanted.

raw: As their wine was measuring out, a man parted from another man in a corner, and rose to depart.
en: As their wine was being poured, a man in the corner said goodbye to his friend and got up to leave.

raw: In going, he had to face Miss Pross.
en: To walk out, he had to face Miss Pross.

raw: No sooner did he face her, than Miss Pross uttered a scream, and clapped her hands.
en: The moment she saw his face, she screamed and clapped her hands.

raw: In a moment, the whole company were on their feet.
en: Instantly, everyone in the shop stood up.

raw: That somebody was assassinated by somebody vindicating a difference of opinion was the likeliest occurrence.
en: They assumed someone had been murdered over a political argument, as that was a common occurrence.

raw: Everybody looked to see somebody fall, but only saw a man and a woman standing staring at each other; the man with all the outward aspect of a Frenchman and a thorough Republican; the woman, evidently English.
en: Everyone looked around for a body, but they only saw a man and a woman staring at each other. The man looked like a typical French Republican, while the woman was clearly English.

raw: What was said in this disappointing anti-climax, by the disciples of the Good Republican Brutus of Antiquity, except that it was something very voluble and loud, would have been as so much Hebrew or Chaldean to Miss Pross and her protector, though they had been all ears.
en: Whatever was being shouted loudly and rapidly by the disappointed followers of the Republic would have sounded like complete gibberish to Miss Pross and her companion, even if they had been listening closely.

raw: But, they had no ears for anything in their surprise.
en: But the two were too surprised to pay attention.

raw: For, it must be recorded, that not only was Miss Pross lost in amazement and agitation, but, Mr. Cruncher--though it seemed on his own separate and individual account--was in a state of the greatest wonder.
en: Not only was Miss Pross shocked and upset, but Jerry Cruncher, for his own secret reasons, was staring in absolute disbelief.

raw: “What is the matter?” said the man who had caused Miss Pross to scream; speaking in a vexed, abrupt voice (though in a low tone), and in English.
en: “What is the matter?” said the man who had made Miss Pross scream. He spoke in a quiet, annoyed voice in English.

raw: “Oh, Solomon, dear Solomon!” cried Miss Pross, clapping her hands again. “After not setting eyes upon you or hearing of you for so long a time, do I find you here!”
en: “Oh, Solomon, dear Solomon!” cried Miss Pross, clapping her hands again. “After not seeing you or hearing from you for so long, to find you here!”

raw: “Don’t call me Solomon.
en: “Don't call me Solomon.

raw: Do you want to be the death of me?” asked the man, in a furtive, frightened way.
en: Do you want to get me killed?” the man asked in a quiet, frightened way.

raw: “Brother, brother!” cried Miss Pross, bursting into tears. “Have I ever been so hard with you that you ask me such a cruel question?”
en: “Brother, brother!” cried Miss Pross, bursting into tears. “Have I ever been so mean to you that you ask me such a cruel question?”

raw: “Then hold your meddlesome tongue,” said Solomon, “and come out, if you want to speak to me.
en: “Then hold your tongue,” Solomon said, “and come outside if you want to talk to me.

raw: Pay for your wine, and come out.
en: Pay for your wine and come out.

raw: Who’s this man?”
en: Who is this man?”

raw: Miss Pross, shaking her loving and dejected head at her by no means affectionate brother, said through her tears, “Mr.
en: Miss Pross, shaking her head sadly at her cold brother, said through her tears, “Mr.

raw: Cruncher.”
en: Cruncher.”

raw: “Let him come out too,” said Solomon. “Does he think me a ghost?”
en: “Let him come out too,” Solomon said. “Does he think I am a ghost?”

raw: Apparently, Mr.
en: Judging by Jerry's face, he definitely did.

raw: Cruncher did, to judge from his looks.
en: He said nothing.

raw: He said not a word, however, and Miss Pross, exploring the depths of her reticule through her tears with great difficulty paid for her wine.
en: Miss Pross searched through her purse, tears streaming, and paid for the wine.

raw: As she did so, Solomon turned to the followers of the Good Republican Brutus of Antiquity, and offered a few words of explanation in the French language, which caused them all to relapse into their former places and pursuits.
en: As she did so, Solomon turned to the other customers and said a few words in French to explain, which made everyone go back to their cards and drinks.

raw: “Now,” said Solomon, stopping at the dark street corner, “what do you want?”
en: “Now,” Solomon said, stopping at a dark corner, “what do you want?”

raw: “How dreadfully unkind in a brother nothing has ever turned my love away from!” cried Miss Pross, “to give me such a greeting, and show me no affection.”
en: “How unkind of a brother whom I have always loved!” cried Miss Pross. “To greet me like this and show no affection at all.”

raw: “There. Confound it!
en: “Fine, damn it!

raw: There,” said Solomon, making a dab at Miss Pross’s lips with his own. “Now are you content?”
en: There,” Solomon said, giving her a quick kiss on the lips. “Are you happy now?”

raw: Miss Pross only shook her head and wept in silence.
en: Miss Pross only shook her head and cried quietly.

raw: “If you expect me to be surprised,” said her brother Solomon, “I am not surprised; I knew you were here; I know of most people who are here.
en: “If you expect me to be surprised, I am not,” her brother Solomon said. “I knew you were here; I know about most people who are in Paris.

raw: If you really don’t want to endanger my existence--which I half believe you do--go your ways as soon as possible, and let me go mine.
en: If you really don't want to put my life in danger, which I think you might, leave as soon as possible and let me go my way.

raw: I am busy.
en: I am busy.

raw: I am an official.”
en: I am a government official.”

raw: “My English brother Solomon,” mourned Miss Pross, casting up her tear-fraught eyes, “that had the makings in him of one of the best and greatest of men in his native country, an official among foreigners, and such foreigners!
en: “My English brother Solomon,” Miss Pross wept, looking up with tearful eyes. “He had the potential to be a great man in his own country, and now he is an official among foreigners, and such terrible foreigners!

raw: I would almost sooner have seen the dear boy lying in his--”
en: I would almost rather have seen him lying in his, ”

raw: “I said so!” cried her brother, interrupting. “I knew it.
en: “I knew it!” her brother interrupted. “You want to get me killed.

raw: You want to be the death of me. I shall be rendered Suspected, by my own sister. Just as I am getting on!”
en: You will make me a 'suspected' person, my own sister, just as I am getting ahead!”

raw: “The gracious and merciful Heavens forbid!” cried Miss Pross. “Far rather would I never see you again, dear Solomon, though I have ever loved you truly, and ever shall.
en: “Heaven forbid!” cried Miss Pross. “I would rather never see you again, dear Solomon, even though I have always loved you.

raw: Say but one affectionate word to me, and tell me there is nothing angry or estranged between us, and I will detain you no longer.”
en: Just say one kind word to me, tell me you aren't angry with me, and I will let you go.”

raw: Good Miss Pross!
en: Good Miss Pross!

raw: As if the estrangement between them had come of any culpability of hers.
en: As if their estrangement were her fault, when Mr.

raw: As if Mr. Lorry had not known it for a fact, years ago, in the quiet corner in Soho, that this precious brother had spent her money and left her!
en: Lorry knew for a fact years ago in London that this worthless brother had stolen all her savings and abandoned her!

raw: He was saying the affectionate word, however, with a far more grudging condescension and patronage than he could have shown if their relative merits and positions had been reversed (which is invariably the case, all the world over), when Mr. Cruncher, touching him on the shoulder, hoarsely and unexpectedly interposed with the following singular question:
en: He was saying a cold, patronizing word to her, looking down on her even though he was the one in the wrong, when Jerry Cruncher touched him on the shoulder and hoarsely asked a very strange question:

raw: “I say! Might I ask the favour?
en: “Excuse me, but could I ask a favor?

en: Is your name John Solomon, or Solomon John?”

en: The official turned to him with sudden suspicion.

raw: He had not previously uttered a word.
en: Jerry had not said a single word until now.

en: “Come on,” Jerry said. “Speak up, you know,” which was hard for Jerry to do with his rough throat. “John Solomon, or Solomon John?

en: She calls you Solomon, so she must know since she is your sister.

en: But _I_ know you are John.

en: Which name goes first?

en: And what about that name Pross?

en: That wasn't your name back in England.”

en: “What do you mean?”

raw: “Well, I don’t know all I mean, for I can’t call to mind what your name was, over the water.”
en: “Well, I don't know exactly, because I can't quite remember what your name was back in England.”

raw: “No?”
en: “No?”

en: “No.

en: But I swear it was a two-syllable name.”

en: I know you.

en: You were a spy witness at the Old Bailey court.

en: What in the name of the devil himself did you call yourself back then?"

raw: “Barsad,” said another voice, striking in.
en: “Barsad,” said another voice, interrupting them.

raw: “That’s the name for a thousand pound!” cried Jerry.
en: “That's the name! I'd bet a thousand pounds on it!” Jerry cried.

raw: The speaker who struck in, was Sydney Carton.
en: The speaker was Sydney Carton.

raw: He had his hands behind him under the skirts of his riding-coat, and he stood at Mr. Cruncher’s elbow as negligently as he might have stood at the Old Bailey itself.
en: He stood with his hands behind him under his coat, leaning next to Jerry as casually as if he were back in the London courtroom.

raw: “Don’t be alarmed, my dear Miss Pross.
en: “Don't be scared, my dear Miss Pross.

raw: I arrived at Mr.
en: I arrived at Mr.

raw: Lorry’s, to his surprise, yesterday evening; we agreed that I would not present myself elsewhere until all was well, or unless I could be useful; I present myself here, to beg a little talk with your brother.
en: Lorry's yesterday evening, surprising him. We agreed I would stay hidden until everything was resolved or I could be useful.

raw: I wish you had a better employed brother than Mr.
en: I am here now to ask for a quiet chat with your brother.

raw: Barsad.
en: I wish your brother had a more honest job, Mr.

en: Barsad.

en: I wish for your sake he wasn't a spy in the prisons.”

raw: Sheep was a cant word of the time for a spy, under the gaolers.
en: "Sheep" was slang at the time for a prison spy.

raw: The spy, who was pale, turned paler, and asked him how he dared--
en: The spy, who was already pale, turned even whiter and asked Carton how he dared,

raw: “I’ll tell you,” said Sydney. “I lighted on you, Mr.
en: “I will tell you,” Sydney said. “I saw you, Mr.

raw: Barsad, coming out of the prison of the Conciergerie while I was contemplating the walls, an hour or more ago.
en: Barsad, coming out of the Conciergerie prison about an hour ago while I was looking at the walls.

raw: You have a face to be remembered, and I remember faces well.
en: You have a memorable face, and I remember faces well.

raw: Made curious by seeing you in that connection, and having a reason, to which you are no stranger, for associating you with the misfortunes of a friend now very unfortunate, I walked in your direction.
en: Curious to see you there, and knowing you were involved in the trial of a friend who is now in great trouble, I followed you.

raw: I walked into the wine-shop here, close after you, and sat near you.
en: I came into this wine shop right after you and sat nearby.

raw: I had no difficulty in deducing from your unreserved conversation, and the rumour openly going about among your admirers, the nature of your calling.
en: Listening to you talk openly and hearing the rumors from the people around you, it was easy to figure out your job.

raw: And gradually, what I had done at random, seemed to shape itself into a purpose, Mr.
en: Gradually, my curiosity turned into a plan, Mr.

en: Barsad.”

en: “What plan?” the spy asked.

en: “It would be difficult and dangerous to explain in the street.

en: Could you join me for a few minutes in private, at Tellson's Bank, for example?”

en: “Is that a threat?”

en: “Oh!

en: Did I say that?”

en: “Then why should I go?”

en: “Really, Mr.

en: Barsad, if you don't know, I can't tell you.”

en: “Do you mean you won't tell me, sir?” the spy asked hesitantly.

raw: “You apprehend me very clearly, Mr.
en: “You understand me perfectly, Mr.

raw: Barsad.
en: Barsad.

en: I won't.”

raw: Carton’s negligent recklessness of manner came powerfully in aid of his quickness and skill, in such a business as he had in his secret mind, and with such a man as he had to do with.
en: Carton's careless and relaxed attitude perfectly hid his quick thinking and skill. This was a great advantage for the secret plan he had in mind, especially when dealing with a man like Barsad.

raw: His practised eye saw it, and made the most of it.
en: His sharp eyes saw the spy's fear and took advantage of it.

raw: “Now, I told you so,” said the spy, casting a reproachful look at his sister; “if any trouble comes of this, it’s your doing.”
en: “See, I told you so,” the spy said, looking at his sister angrily. “If I get into trouble, it is your fault.”

raw: “Come, come, Mr.
en: “Come, come, Mr.

raw: Barsad!” exclaimed Sydney. “Don’t be ungrateful.
en: Barsad!” Sydney said. “Don't be ungrateful.

raw: But for my great respect for your sister, I might not have led up so pleasantly to a little proposal that I wish to make for our mutual satisfaction.
en: Out of respect for your sister, I have been polite about the proposal I want to make.

raw: Do you go with me to the Bank?”
en: Are you coming to the bank with me?”

raw: “I’ll hear what you have got to say.
en: “I'll hear what you have to say.

en: Yes, I'll go with you.”

raw: “I propose that we first conduct your sister safely to the corner of her own street.
en: “First, let's walk your sister safely to the corner of her street.

raw: Let me take your arm, Miss Pross.
en: May I take your arm, Miss Pross?

en: Paris is not a safe city for you to walk around alone right now. Since your guard knows Mr.

en: Barsad, I will invite him to Mr.

en: Lorry's with us.

raw: Are we ready?
en: Ready?

raw: Come then!”
en: Let's go!”

raw: Miss Pross recalled soon afterwards, and to the end of her life remembered, that as she pressed her hands on Sydney’s arm and looked up in his face, imploring him to do no hurt to Solomon, there was a braced purpose in the arm and a kind of inspiration in the eyes, which not only contradicted his light manner, but changed and raised the man.
en: Miss Pross remembered this moment for the rest of her life. When she held Sydney's arm and begged him not to hurt Solomon, his arm felt strong and steady. His eyes looked inspired, completely different from his usual lazy, careless look.

raw: She was too much occupied then with fears for the brother who so little deserved her affection, and with Sydney’s friendly reassurances, adequately to heed what she observed.
en: She was too worried about her worthless brother to dwell on it much then. And Sydney's kind words comforted her too much to let her think clearly.

raw: They left her at the corner of the street, and Carton led the way to Mr.
en: They left her at the corner, and Carton led the way to Mr.

raw: Lorry’s, which was within a few minutes’ walk.
en: Lorry's place, which was only a few minutes' walk away.

raw: John Barsad, or Solomon Pross, walked at his side.
en: John Barsad, also known as Solomon Pross, walked next to him.

en: Mr.

raw: Lorry had just finished his dinner, and was sitting before a cheery little log or two of fire--perhaps looking into their blaze for the picture of that younger elderly gentleman from Tellson’s, who had looked into the red coals at the Royal George at Dover, now a good many years ago.
en: Lorry had just finished dinner and sat before a cozy fire, perhaps remembering himself as a younger man at the inn in Dover many years ago.

raw: He turned his head as they entered, and showed the surprise with which he saw a stranger.
en: He turned around as they entered, looking surprised to see a stranger.

en: Barsad.”

en: I remember that name, and that face.”

en: Barsad,” Carton remarked calmly. “Please sit down.”

en: Lorry remembered immediately and looked at the visitor with clear disgust.

en: “Mr.

raw: Barsad has been recognised by Miss Pross as the affectionate brother you have heard of,” said Sydney, “and has acknowledged the relationship. I pass to worse news.
en: Barsad has been recognized by Miss Pross as her brother, and he has admitted it,” Sydney said. “Now, here is the bad news.

raw: Darnay has been arrested again.”
en: Darnay has been arrested again.”

raw: Struck with consternation, the old gentleman exclaimed, “What do you tell me!
en: Shocked, Mr. Lorry cried out, “What are you saying!

en: I left him safe and free just two hours ago, and I was about to go back to see him!”

en: “Just now, if it's true.”

en: “Mr.

raw: There is no earthly doubt that he is retaken.”

en: Mr.

en: Though confused, he knew he had to keep his head clear, so he calmed himself and listened quietly.

raw: “Now, I trust,” said Sydney to him, “that the name and influence of Doctor Manette may stand him in as good stead to-morrow--you said he would be before the Tribunal again to-morrow, Mr.
en: “Now, I hope,” Sydney said to Mr. Lorry, “that Doctor Manette's influence will help him tomorrow. You said he would be tried again tomorrow, Mr.

en: “But that fact itself is alarming, considering how close he is to his son-in-law.”

en: "He continued like a man laying down his cards one by one.

raw: Barsad,” he went on, in the tone of one who really was looking over a hand at cards: “Sheep of the prisons, emissary of Republican committees, now turnkey, now prisoner, always spy and secret informer, so much the more valuable here for being English that an Englishman is less open to suspicion of subornation in those characters than a Frenchman, represents himself to his employers under a false name.
en: "Mr. Barsad," Carton continued, talking as if he were studying a hand of cards, "is a prison spy, a messenger for Republican committees, sometimes acting as a guard and sometimes as a prisoner. He is always a secret informer, and he is especially valuable here because an Englishman is less likely to be suspected of being a spy than a Frenchman. He even uses a fake name with his bosses."

raw: That’s a very good card.
en: You are extra valuable because you are English, meaning you look less suspicious.

raw: Mr.
en: But you are using a fake name.

raw: Barsad, now in the employ of the republican French government, was formerly in the employ of the aristocratic English government, the enemy of France and freedom.
en: Mr. Barsad, who now works for the French Republican government, used to work for the English government—the very enemy of France and freedom.

raw: That’s an excellent card.
en: You currently work for the French Republic, but you used to work for the English government, France's enemy.

raw: Inference clear as day in this region of suspicion, that Mr.
en: In this land of constant suspicion, the conclusion is clear as day: Mr.

raw: Barsad, still in the pay of the aristocratic English government, is the spy of Pitt, the treacherous foe of the Republic crouching in its bosom, the English traitor and agent of all mischief so much spoken of and so difficult to find.
en: In this suspicious city, everyone will assume that you are still in the pay of England, a spy for Pitt, a traitor hiding in the heart of France.

raw: That’s a card not to be beaten.
en: That card cannot be beaten.

raw: Have you followed my hand, Mr.
en: Do you see my cards, Mr.

raw: Barsad?”
en: Barsad?”

raw: “Not to understand your play,” returned the spy, somewhat uneasily.
en: “I don't understand what you are playing at,” the spy said nervously.

raw: “I play my Ace, Denunciation of Mr. Barsad to the nearest Section Committee.
en: “I am playing my Ace: reporting you to the nearest revolutionary committee.

raw: Look over your hand, Mr.
en: Look at your own cards, Mr.

raw: Barsad, and see what you have.
en: Barsad, and see what you have.

raw: Don’t hurry.”
en: Take your time.”

raw: He drew the bottle near, poured out another glassful of brandy, and drank it off.
en: He poured another glass of brandy and drank it.

raw: He saw that the spy was fearful of his drinking himself into a fit state for the immediate denunciation of him. Seeing it, he poured out and drank another glassful.
en: He saw the spy was worried Carton would drink enough to get angry and report him immediately, so Carton deliberately drank another glass.

raw: “Look over your hand carefully, Mr.
en: “Look at your hand carefully, Mr.

raw: Barsad.
en: Barsad.

raw: Take time.”
en: Take your time.”

raw: It was a poorer hand than he suspected.
en: The spy's hand was even worse than Carton realized, containing secrets Carton didn't even know.

raw: Mr. Barsad saw losing cards in it that Sydney Carton knew nothing of.
en: Having lost his job in England because his lies in court were exposed, he had come to France to work as a spy, first spying on English exiles, then on the French citizens.

raw: Thrown out of his honourable employment in England, through too much unsuccessful hard swearing there--not because he was not wanted there; our English reasons for vaunting our superiority to secrecy and spies are of very modern date--he knew that he had crossed the Channel, and accepted service in France: first, as a tempter and an eavesdropper among his own countrymen there: gradually, as a tempter and an eavesdropper among the natives.
en: After losing his respectable job in England because of too much obvious lying in court, he had crossed the English Channel to work in France. First, he spied and eavesdropped on his own countrymen there, and later he started spying on the French locals.

raw: He knew that under the overthrown government he had been a spy upon Saint Antoine and Defarge’s wine-shop; had received from the watchful police such heads of information concerning Doctor Manette’s imprisonment, release, and history, as should serve him for an introduction to familiar conversation with the Defarges; and tried them on Madame Defarge, and had broken down with them signally.
en: He knew that under the old government, he had spied on the Saint Antoine neighborhood and Defarge's wine shop. The police had given him enough details about Doctor Manette's imprisonment and release to help him start a conversation with the Defarges. He had tried to use this information on Madame Defarge, but he had failed completely.

raw: He always remembered with fear and trembling, that that terrible woman had knitted when he talked with her, and had looked ominously at him as her fingers moved.
en: He remembered with terror how Madame Defarge had knitted while talking to him, looking at him coldly.

raw: He had since seen her, in the Section of Saint Antoine, over and over again produce her knitted registers, and denounce people whose lives the guillotine then surely swallowed up.
en: Since then, he had seen her in the neighborhood meetings pointing to her knitting to accuse people who were then executed.

raw: He knew, as every one employed as he was did, that he was never safe; that flight was impossible; that he was tied fast under the shadow of the axe; and that in spite of his utmost tergiversation and treachery in furtherance of the reigning terror, a word might bring it down upon him.
en: Like everyone in his line of work, he knew that he was never truly safe and that escaping was impossible. He was trapped under the constant threat of the Guillotine. Despite all his lying and plotting to support the Reign of Terror, just one wrong word could bring the axe down on his own neck.

raw: Once denounced, and on such grave grounds as had just now been suggested to his mind, he foresaw that the dreadful woman of whose unrelenting character he had seen many proofs, would produce against him that fatal register, and would quash his last chance of life.
en: If he were ever reported for the serious crimes Carton just mentioned, he knew exactly what would happen. That terrifying woman, whose ruthless nature he had seen many times, would bring out her deadly knitted records to destroy his final chance of surviving.

raw: Besides that all secret men are men soon terrified, here were surely cards enough of one black suit, to justify the holder in growing rather livid as he turned them over.
en: Men who live a life of secrets are easily terrified, and this hand of cards was certainly dark enough to make anyone turn pale with fear as they were played.

raw: “You scarcely seem to like your hand,” said Sydney, with the greatest composure. “Do you play?”
en: “You don't seem to like your cards,” Sydney said calmly. “Are you going to play?”

raw: “I think, sir,” said the spy, in the meanest manner, as he turned to Mr.
en: "I think, sir," said the spy in a very cowardly way, as he turned toward Mr.

raw: Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your years and benevolence, to put it to this other gentleman, so much your junior, whether he can under any circumstances reconcile it to his station to play that Ace of which he has spoken.
en: Lorry with a groveling tone. "I think, sir, I can ask a kind gentleman of your age to ask this younger man if he really thinks it is right to report me.

raw: I admit that _I_ am a spy, and that it is considered a discreditable station--though it must be filled by somebody; but this gentleman is no spy, and why should he so demean himself as to make himself one?”
en: I admit I am a spy, and that it's a dirty job, though someone has to do it. But this gentleman is not a spy, so why should he lower himself to act like one?”

raw: “I play my Ace, Mr.
en: Carton looked at his watch.

raw: Barsad,” said Carton, taking the answer on himself, and looking at his watch, “without any scruple, in a very few minutes.”
en: He answered, "I am playing my Ace, Mr. Barsad, without any hesitation, in just a few minutes."”

raw: “I should have hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, always striving to hook Mr.
en: "The spy tried once more, this time turning his eyes to Mr. Lorry to pull him into the conversation.

raw: Lorry into the discussion, “that your respect for my sister--”
en: "I hoped, gentlemen, that out of respect for my sister, "”

raw: “I could not better testify my respect for your sister than by finally relieving her of her brother,” said Sydney Carton. “You think not, sir?”
en: “I couldn't show more respect for your sister than by freeing her of her brother once and for all,” said Sydney Carton.

raw: “I have thoroughly made up my mind about it.”
en: "I am completely certain about it."

raw: The smooth manner of the spy, curiously in dissonance with his ostentatiously rough dress, and probably with his usual demeanour, received such a check from the inscrutability of Carton,--who was a mystery to wiser and honester men than he,--that it faltered here and failed him.
en: The spy's smooth and polite manners strangely didn't match his deliberately rough clothes or his usual behavior. However, his confident act hit a wall against Carton's completely unreadable face. Carton was a mystery to men much smarter and more honest than the spy, so Barsad quickly lost his nerve and his smooth manner failed him entirely.

raw: While he was at a loss, Carton said, resuming his former air of contemplating cards:
en: Not knowing what to do, the spy remained quiet while Carton spoke again, looking at his imaginary cards:

raw: “And indeed, now I think again, I have a strong impression that I have another good card here, not yet enumerated.
en: “And indeed, now I think again, I have a strong impression that I have another good card here, not yet enumerated.

raw: That friend and fellow-Sheep, who spoke of himself as pasturing in the country prisons; who was he?”
en: That friend and fellow-Sheep, who spoke of himself as pasturing in the country prisons; who was he?”

raw: “French.
en: “He is French.

raw: You don’t know him,” said the spy, quickly.
en: You don't know him,” the spy said quickly.

raw: “French, eh?” repeated Carton, musing, and not appearing to notice him at all, though he echoed his word. “Well; he may be.”
en: “French, is he?” Carton repeated thoughtfully, looking away. “Well, maybe he is.”

raw: “Is, I assure you,” said the spy; “though it’s not important.”
en: “He is, I assure you,” said the spy, “though it doesn't matter.”

raw: “Though it’s not important,” repeated Carton, in the same mechanical way--“though it’s not important--No, it’s not important.
en: “Though it doesn't matter,” Carton repeated slowly. “No, it doesn't matter.

raw: No. Yet I know the face.”
en: But I know his face.”

raw: “I think not.
en: “I think not.

raw: I am sure not.
en: I am sure you don't.

raw: It can’t be,” said the spy.
en: It's impossible,” said the spy.

raw: “It-can’t-be,” muttered Sydney Carton, retrospectively, and idling his glass (which fortunately was a small one) again. “Can’t-be.
en: “It's impossible,” Sydney Carton muttered, spinning his glass. “Impossible.

raw: Spoke good French. Yet like a foreigner, I thought?”
en: He spoke good French, but he sounded like a foreigner, didn't he?”

raw: “Provincial,” said the spy.
en: “He just has an accent from the countryside,” said the spy.

raw: “No. Foreign!” cried Carton, striking his open hand on the table, as a light broke clearly on his mind. “Cly!
en: “No, he is a foreigner!” Carton cried, hitting the table as he suddenly realized the truth. “It is Roger Cly!

raw: Disguised, but the same man.
en: He is in disguise, but it's him.

raw: We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”
en: We saw him at the trial in London.”

raw: “Now, there you are hasty, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that gave his aquiline nose an extra inclination to one side; “there you really give me an advantage over you.
en: "Now, you are being a bit too quick to judge, sir," said Barsad, offering a smile that made his sharp nose tilt even more to one side. "By saying that, you've actually given me an advantage over you."

raw: Cly (who I will unreservedly admit, at this distance of time, was a partner of mine) has been dead several years.
en: Cly, who was my partner, I admit now, has been dead for years.

raw: I attended him in his last illness.
en: I was with him when he died.

raw: He was buried in London, at the church of Saint Pancras-in-the-Fields.
en: He was buried in London at Saint Pancras Church.

raw: His unpopularity with the blackguard multitude at the moment prevented my following his remains, but I helped to lay him in his coffin.”
en: The crowd hated him so much that I couldn't attend the funeral service, but I helped put him in his coffin.”

raw: Here, Mr.
en: Here, Mr.

raw: Lorry became aware, from where he sat, of a most remarkable goblin shadow on the wall.
en: Lorry noticed a strange, spiky shadow on the wall.

raw: Tracing it to its source, he discovered it to be caused by a sudden extraordinary rising and stiffening of all the risen and stiff hair on Mr. Cruncher’s head.
en: Looking over, he saw it was caused by all the hair on Jerry Cruncher's head standing straight up in excitement.

raw: “Let us be reasonable,” said the spy, “and let us be fair. To show you how mistaken you are, and what an unfounded assumption yours is, I will lay before you a certificate of Cly’s burial, which I happened to have carried in my pocket-book,” with a hurried hand he produced and opened it, “ever since. There it is.
en: “Let's be reasonable,” the spy said. “To show you that you are wrong, I have Cly's burial certificate right here in my wallet.” He quickly pulled it out. “Here it is.

raw: Oh, look at it, look at it!
en: Look at it.

raw: You may take it in your hand; it’s no forgery.”
en: You can hold it; it is real.”

raw: Here, Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry perceived the reflection on the wall to elongate, and Mr. Cruncher rose and stepped forward.
en: Lorry saw the shadow move, and Jerry Cruncher stepped forward.

raw: His hair could not have been more violently on end, if it had been that moment dressed by the Cow with the crumpled horn in the house that Jack built.
en: His spiky hair was standing on end as if he had been shocked by electricity.

raw: Unseen by the spy, Mr. Cruncher stood at his side, and touched him on the shoulder like a ghostly bailiff.
en: Without the spy seeing him, Jerry stood at his side and tapped his shoulder like a ghost.

raw: “That there Roger Cly, master,” said Mr. Cruncher, with a taciturn and iron-bound visage. “So _you_ put him in his coffin?”
en: “That Roger Cly,” Jerry said with a grim face. “So _you_ put him in his coffin?”

raw: “I did.”
en: “I did.”

raw: “Who took him out of it?”
en: “Then who took him out of it?”

raw: Barsad leaned back in his chair, and stammered, “What do you mean?”
en: Barsad leaned back and stammered, “What do you mean?”

raw: “I mean,” said Mr. Cruncher, “that he warn’t never in it.
en: “I mean,” Jerry said, “that he was never in it!

raw: No! Not he!
en: No, not him!

raw: I’ll have my head took off, if he was ever in it.”
en: I will lose my head if he was ever in that coffin.”

raw: The spy looked round at the two gentlemen; they both looked in unspeakable astonishment at Jerry.
en: The spy looked at Carton and Lorry, who were both staring at Jerry in absolute surprise.

raw: “I tell you,” said Jerry, “that you buried paving-stones and earth in that there coffin.
en: “I tell you,” Jerry said, “that you buried paving stones and dirt in that coffin.

raw: Don’t go and tell me that you buried Cly.
en: Don't tell me you buried Cly.

raw: It was a take in.
en: It was a trick.

raw: Me and two more knows it.”
en: I and two other men know it.”

raw: “How do you know it?”
en: “How do you know that?”

raw: “What’s that to you?
en: “What is that to you?

raw: Ecod!” growled Mr. Cruncher, “it’s you I have got a old grudge again, is it, with your shameful impositions upon tradesmen!
en: Damn!” Jerry growled. “So it's you I have an old grudge against, with your trickery!

raw: I’d catch hold of your throat and choke you for half a guinea.”
en: I'd choke you right now for half a coin.”

raw: Sydney Carton, who, with Mr. Lorry, had been lost in amazement at this turn of the business, here requested Mr.
en: Sydney Carton, who had been just as amazed as Mr. Lorry by this unexpected turn of events, now asked Mr.

raw: Cruncher to moderate and explain himself.
en: Lorry, told Jerry to calm down and explain.

raw: “At another time, sir,” he returned, evasively, “the present time is ill-conwenient for explainin’. What I stand to, is, that he knows well wot that there Cly was never in that there coffin.
en: “Some other time, sir,” Jerry replied, avoiding the question. “Right now is not a good time to explain.

raw: Let him say he was, in so much as a word of one syllable, and I’ll either catch hold of his throat and choke him for half a guinea;” Mr.
en: All I say is that he knows very well Cly was never in that coffin.

raw: Cruncher dwelt upon this as quite a liberal offer; “or I’ll out and announce him.”
en: Let him deny it, and I will choke him, or I will go and report him to the police.”

raw: “Humph! I see one thing,” said Carton. “I hold another card, Mr.
en: “Well, I see one thing,” Carton said. “I have another card, Mr.

raw: Barsad.
en: Barsad.

raw: Impossible, here in raging Paris, with Suspicion filling the air, for you to outlive denunciation, when you are in communication with another aristocratic spy of the same antecedents as yourself, who, moreover, has the mystery about him of having feigned death and come to life again!
en: It is impossible for you to survive in Paris if I report you for working with another English spy who faked his death.

raw: A plot in the prisons, of the foreigner against the Republic.
en: They will call it a foreign plot in the prisons against the Republic.

raw: A strong card--a certain Guillotine card!
en: That is a winning card, a Guillotine card!

raw: Do you play?”
en: Do you play?”

raw: “No!” returned the spy. “I throw up.
en: “No!” the spy replied. “I give up.

raw: I confess that we were so unpopular with the outrageous mob, that I only got away from England at the risk of being ducked to death, and that Cly was so ferreted up and down, that he never would have got away at all but for that sham.
en: I'll admit that we were so hated by the wild mobs in England that I barely escaped with my life. Cly was hunted so relentlessly that he never would have gotten away at all if he hadn't faked his own death.

raw: Though how this man knows it was a sham, is a wonder of wonders to me.”
en: How this man knows it was a trick is a mystery to me.”

raw: “Never you trouble your head about this man,” retorted the contentious Mr. Cruncher; “you’ll have trouble enough with giving your attention to that gentleman. And look here! Once more!”--Mr.
en: "Don't you worry your head about me," argued an angry Mr. Cruncher. "You'll have more than enough trouble just dealing with that gentleman right there. And look here! I'll tell you one more time!" — Mr.

raw: Cruncher could not be restrained from making rather an ostentatious parade of his liberality--“I’d catch hold of your throat and choke you for half a guinea.”
en: Cruncher just couldn't resist showing off how generous he felt — "I'd grab you by the throat and choke the life out of you for just half a guinea."

raw: The Sheep of the prisons turned from him to Sydney Carton, and said, with more decision, “It has come to a point.
en: The spy turned back to Carton and said, “Let's get to the point.

raw: I go on duty soon, and can’t overstay my time.
en: I have to go on duty soon.

raw: You told me you had a proposal; what is it?
en: You mentioned that you had a proposal for me; what exactly is it?

raw: Now, it is of no use asking too much of me.
en: Don't ask too much of me.

raw: Ask me to do anything in my office, putting my head in great extra danger, and I had better trust my life to the chances of a refusal than the chances of consent.
en: If you ask me to help someone escape, which puts my head on the line, I'd rather refuse.

raw: In short, I should make that choice. You talk of desperation.
en: To put it simply, that is the choice I would make. Now, you mentioned being desperate.

raw: We are all desperate here. Remember! I may denounce you if I think proper, and I can swear my way through stone walls, and so can others.
en: Remember, I can report you too, and I can lie in court to protect myself.

raw: Now, what do you want with me?”
en: What do you want?”

raw: “Not very much.
en: “Not much.

raw: You are a turnkey at the Conciergerie?”
en: You are a guard at the Conciergerie?”

raw: “I tell you once for all, there is no such thing as an escape possible,”  said the spy, firmly.
en: “I tell you now, an escape is completely impossible,” the spy said firmly.

raw: “Why need you tell me what I have not asked?
en: “Why are you telling me what I didn't ask?

raw: You are a turnkey at the Conciergerie?”
en: You are a guard at the Conciergerie?”

raw: “I am sometimes.”
en: “Sometimes.”

raw: “You can be when you choose?”
en: “You can get inside when you choose?”

raw: “I can pass in and out when I choose.”
en: “I can go in and out when I choose.”

raw: Sydney Carton filled another glass with brandy, poured it slowly out upon the hearth, and watched it as it dropped.
en: Sydney Carton filled another glass with brandy, poured it slowly onto the hearth, and watched it drip away.

raw: It being all spent, he said, rising:
en: Once the glass was empty, he stood up and said:

raw: “So far, we have spoken before these two, because it was as well that the merits of the cards should not rest solely between you and me.
en: “We spoke in front of these two so they could witness the cards I hold.

raw: Come into the dark room here, and let us have one final word alone.”
en: Now, come into this back room, and let's have one final word alone.”
